questions.q: What does a switch do the first time it receives a frame addressed to a MAC address it hasn't learned yet?
options: It floods the frame out every port except the one it arrived on
It drops the frame silently
It sends the frame to its default gateway
It converts the frame into an IP packet and routes it
questions.explain: Unknown unicast flooding: the switch sends the frame everywhere except where it came from, then learns the real MAC-to-port mapping from the reply.

questions.q: What does a router use to decide where to forward a packet?
options: The packet's source MAC address
The packet's destination IP address, matched against a routing table using longest prefix match
A VLAN tag only
The frame's checksum
questions.explain: A router's core forwarding decision is Layer 3: it compares the destination IP against its routing table and picks the most specific matching entry.

questions.q: What is the real difference between a collision domain and a broadcast domain?
options: They're two names for the same thing
A collision domain is the set of devices whose transmissions can collide (one per switch port); a broadcast domain is the set of devices that receive a broadcast, which a switch never shrinks
A broadcast domain only exists inside a single switch port
A collision domain is broken up by routers, and a broadcast domain is broken up by switches
questions.explain: Switches give every port its own collision domain, but they flood broadcasts out every port, so a switch never reduces the size of a broadcast domain — only a router does.

questions.q: In the Host A → switch → router → Host B path, what stays exactly the same at every hop while the MAC addresses change?
options: The source and destination IP addresses inside the packet
The MAC addresses
The VLAN ID
The physical cable type
questions.explain: Each router hop rebuilds the Layer 2 frame with new source/destination MAC addresses, but the IP header's source and destination addresses are untouched end to end (absent NAT).

options: The switch port with the highest priority
The router address a host sends traffic to when the destination is off its own subnet
The DNS server configured on a host
The broadcast address of the local subnet
questions.explain: When a host determines the destination isn't on its own subnet, it sends the frame to its default gateway — the router responsible for getting it further along.
